definition: In statistical learning theory, a learnable function class is a set of functions for which an algorithm can be devised to asymptotically minimize the expected risk, uniformly over all probability distributions.
details: The concept of learnable classes are closely related to regularization in machine learning, and provides large sample justifications for certain learning algorithms.

explainer.lead: A learnable function class is a set of functions for which an algorithm can asymptotically minimize expected risk uniformly over all probability distributions. It matters because it explains when a learning algorithm can be justified with large samples.

tiers.eli5: Think of a toolbox of possible rules; a learnable class is a toolbox where, given enough examples, some procedure is guaranteed to find a rule that works well no matter what the world looks like.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use the idea to argue that a chosen model family plus algorithm has large-sample guarantees, and tie it to regularization. A pitfall is assuming a practical finite-data setting behaves like the asymptotic guarantee.
tiers.paperLevel: A class of functions is learnable if there exists an algorithm whose expected risk converges to the minimum over the class, uniformly over all probability distributions. The guarantee is asymptotic, so it says nothing about finite-sample behavior.

explainer.example: If a function class admits an algorithm whose expected risk approaches the best achievable in the class for every distribution as sample size grows, that class is learnable.
